1.pericope_label: The word which came unto Jeremiah from the LORD in the days of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah king of Judah, saying
debates: How far out of order the chapter stands
How long before this Jonadab lived
What the name son of Rechab means
Why the wine was offered in the temple
outliers: Calvin explains the disordered arrangement by an account of how the book was formed, the discourses summarised, posted on the temple doors and laid up in the archives
Ellicott suggests that son of Rechab may mean son of the chariot, that is disciple of the great prophet, since the same word was applied to Elijah
Calvin argues from the priests being allowed wine except while serving, so that the refusal of aliens left the people no excuse
Keil and Delitzsch assign the title man of God to Hanan rather than to his father Jigdaliah
themes: A prophecy that reaches back over a buried reign
The life of cities counted the death of liberty
Property in cattle and tents, easily removed
A good man taken up into the chariot for appearance

3.pericope_label: Then I took Jaazaniah the son of Jeremiah, the son of Habaziniah, and his brethren, and all his sons, and the whole house of the Rechabites
debates: Whether the Rechabites were a family or a religious order
Whether the title man of God belongs to Hanan or to Igdaliah
Whether the prohibition of agriculture can be defended
outliers: Ellicott reads the names as evidence that the Rechabites shared the faith of Israel, and takes brethren and sons for degrees of membership in an order
Calvin explains the choice of the temple by publicity, since a thing done in an obscure corner may be thought doubtful or fabulous
Ellicott takes the sons of Hanan for scholars in training, so that the prophet is introducing two religious orders to each other
Calvin grants that agriculture is of all modes of living the simplest and most innocent, and defends the prohibition only from the circumstances
themes: Names that carry a confession in them
A select place made into a notable theatre
Witnesses drawn from the priestly, prophetic and official orders
An austere life chosen so that little could be lost

6.pericope_label: But they said, We will drink no wine: for Jonadab the son of Rechab our father commanded us, saying, Ye shall drink no wine, neither ye, nor your sons for ever
debates: Whether the precepts carry a meaning beyond the letter
Whether the prohibition falls on building or on dwelling
Why a second army is named beside the Chaldeans
outliers: Clarke gives each of the three precepts a spiritual sense, temperance, freedom from ambition, and the pilgrim life of the patriarchs
Calvin measures the difficulty by the Nazarites and the serving priest, who abstained only for a time, against a whole life without wine
Calvin argues that the discipline proved advantageous, since owning nothing they could move freely and were spared the trial of leaving possessions
Ellicott reads their presence in the city as an apologetic explanation of a temporary casualty
themes: Precepts kept for a man dead three hundred years
Palaces built for others and never lived in
Men who would rather be killed than torn from their fields
Everything a family owns gathered in one day

12.pericope_label: Then came the word of the LORD unto Jeremiah, saying, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Go and tell the men of Judah
debates: When the prophet passed from acting to prophesying
What the word rendered instruction means
Why a hard command was kept and an easy one was not
outliers: Ellicott holds that the prophet acted first on a partial insight and only now passes into the prophetic state, the speech being delivered in the hearing of the Rechabites
Henry stacks three aggravations, the merely human father, the father long dead and powerless, and the reminders never given to the one family and repeatedly given to the other
Calvin contrasts a command given once and remembered for ages with commands repeated early and often and forgotten
Calvin draws from the phrase rising early a rule that those to be ruled by us must be formed from infancy
themes: A man of flesh obeyed and the Father of spirits not
A dead man who could neither notice nor punish
Wine forbidden by no law of God and still refused
All my severity is a rule of meekness

15.pericope_label: I have sent also unto you all my servants the prophets, rising up early and sending them, saying, Return ye now every man from his evil way
debates: Why the prophets had to be sent so often
Whether anything more than natural light was needed
What the change of preposition signifies
outliers: Calvin argues that men otherwise refractory grow gentle when recalled to duty every day and hour, so that refusal under such treatment proves the obstinacy
Calvin holds that natural light alone would have taught the duty, so that every man ought to have been his own teacher
Calvin distinguishes God speaking to a people from God speaking against them, two barely distinguishable prepositions marking doctrine and threatening
Ellicott dates the summons to return to the prophet own earlier preaching in the fourth year, before the incident recorded here
themes: Prophets sent where the other family needed none
A requirement that nature itself dictates
Every means tried and nothing effected
A thunderbolt withheld until the guilt is proved

18.pericope_label: And Jeremiah said unto the house of the Rechabites, Thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; Because ye have obeyed the commandment of Jonadab your father
debates: Whether standing before God means priestly ministration
How long the for ever of the promise runs
Whether the blessing makes the rule binding on others
outliers: Ellicott finds the phrase about standing before God to be a liturgical expression for the ministrations of the Levites, while Calvin calls that inference strained and rejects the application to the priesthood

Calvin limits the approval by holding that obedience to a father in an unlawful thing would have deserved punishment, and that the precept did not bind the conscience since they lived in hired houses when necessity came
Ellicott collects the later appearances of the name, from an early account of a martyrdom to travellers reports of desert tribes claiming the descent
Ellicott praises faithfulness to any rule of life sanctioned by prescription, whether of a school, a college, a guild or a religious order
themes: A human precept praised without being imposed
Tents left behind and hired dwellings taken
A name that keeps cropping up in strange places
Patterns of simplicity and deadness to the world
